slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty: the examination of combination.

slides.heading: What does coming-together do?
points: Bread needs flour, water, yeast, oven, baker
No single one makes bread
Is the bread already in the gathering?
slides.say: A loaf of bread needs flour, water, yeast, an oven and a baker. No single one of them makes bread. Put them together, and bread comes out. So it seems natural to say that the bread is produced by the coming-together of its causes and conditions. This chapter asks what that coming-together actually does. Is the bread already in the gathering? Does the gathering hand something over to it? When the bread appears, are its causes still there, or already gone?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Chapter 1: can single conditions produce?
The reply: not one, but the whole collection
Chapter 20 tests that reply
slides.say: The chapter returns to the question of chapter one from a new side. Chapter one asked whether single conditions can produce an effect. A natural reply is that no single condition does it, but the whole collection does. Chapter twenty tests that reply. It finds that the collection meets every problem the single conditions met, and a few more besides, as long as cause, collection and effect are each taken to exist on their own.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Is the bread already in the gathering?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The opening verses set a simple choice. When flour, water, yeast and heat come together, either the bread is already somehow present in that gathering, or it is not. Suppose it is present. Then it should be found there, in the bowl and the oven, before the baking is done. It is not. And if it were, nothing would be left for the gathering to do: you do not bake a loaf that already exists. Suppose instead it is not present in the gathering at all. Then the gathering has no special link to bread. Flour and yeast would be no more the causes of bread than sand and gravel are, since neither contains it. Anything could come from anything. This is the same fork as in chapter one. It has only been moved from the single conditions to their sum. Adding things together does not help, because the question is not how many causes there are. It is how a cause that stands on its own could reach an effect that stands on its own.

slides.heading: Does the cause hand something over?
points: 20.5: give its power and cease: two selves
20.6: cease without giving: no cause at all
20.9: turn into the effect: born a second time
slides.say: A second way to picture production is as a handover. The seed passes its power to the sprout, then dies away, like a runner handing on a baton. Verses twenty point five and six take this picture at its word. If the cause gives its power to the effect and then ceases, the cause has split into two: the part handed on, which lives in the effect, and the part that ceased. A single thing with its own nature cannot both go on and stop. If instead the cause ceases without handing anything on, the effect appears after its cause is gone, with nothing joining them. That effect would have no cause at all. Verse twenty point nine adds a variant. Perhaps the cause passes over into the effect, like a person moving house. Then nothing new has arisen. The same thing, already born, has simply been born again.

slides.heading: Before, with or after?
slides.say: The next question is about time. When the effect appears, where is its cause? There are only three answers. If the effect appears at the same time as its gathering, then producer and produced exist side by side, and two things both already there do not stand as maker and made: a potter and a finished pot, both on the table, are not in the act of making. If the effect came before its gathering, it owes nothing to causes that come later. And a cause gone before the effect cannot produce anything; it is no longer there to act. Placed on a line of time, a self-standing cause and a self-standing effect either do not overlap, and then nothing connects them, or they overlap, and then both are simply present and nothing is being produced. Verse twenty point eleven closes the loop: a cause does not produce an effect it has never met, and it does not need to produce one it has already met.

slides.heading: Where do cause and effect meet?
slides.say: Production seems to need contact. The match must touch the strip; the seed must be in the soil when the sprout begins. Verses twelve to fourteen test this meeting across the three times, for the cause and for the effect. Two things can meet only if both are there together. Whatever is past is gone; whatever is not yet born has not come. So in eight of the nine pairings one side is missing, and there is nothing to meet. In the remaining case both are present, and they can touch. But then the effect is already there, so the touching does not produce it. That is verse fifteen: without contact, how could a cause produce anything? With contact, what is left for it to produce?

slides.heading: Empty of the effect, or full of it?
points: 20.16: lacking the effect, or containing it?
20.17: a non-empty thing never arises or ceases
20.18: 'empty' as a blank does not help either
slides.say: Verse twenty point sixteen restates the problem with the word empty. Either the cause is empty of the effect, lacking it entirely, or it is full of it. If it lacks it entirely, how can it give rise to it? If it already contains it, how is anything new produced? Verses seventeen and eighteen push one step further. Something that is not empty, in the sense of having its own fixed nature, could never arise or cease. It would simply be what it is, always. But the opponent cannot rescue arising by calling the effect empty, if empty means a kind of nothing. A nothing does not arise or cease either.

slides.heading: A delicate pair of verses
points: Not: emptiness makes arising impossible
Chapter 24: only the empty can arise and cease
Rejected: arising found as an event in things
slides.say: This is a delicate pair of verses. Nagarjuna is not saying that emptiness, rightly understood, makes arising impossible. In chapter twenty-four he says the opposite: only because things are empty can they arise and cease at all. What verse eighteen rejects is arising found under analysis. If empty is taken as a blank, a nothing cannot be produced or destroyed. And even an empty thing, rightly understood, is not found arising or ceasing in its own right when it is looked for; that is why chapter eighteen calls the nature of things unarisen and unceasing. Arising and ceasing are kept, but as dependent designations, not as events found in things.

slides.heading: The same, or different?
slides.say: Verses nineteen and twenty bring in the pair of identity and difference, one of the pairs among the eight extremes of the homage. If cause and effect were one thing, the parent and the child would be the same person, and the seed would be the sprout. Nothing would have been produced. If they were two wholly separate things, the seed would be as unrelated to the sprout as a stone is, and a cause would be no different from a non-cause. Identity removes the difference between maker and made; difference removes the link that makes this the cause rather than any other thing. Rice comes from rice seed and not from barley, which already shows that the relation is neither sameness nor separateness.

slides.heading: Without an effect, no cause
points: 20.21: an effect existent or non-existent by nature
20.22: what produces nothing is no cause
20.24: no effect, so no 'gathering' either
slides.say: The last verses gather the threads. If the effect exists by its own nature, it is already there, and a cause has nothing to do. If its very nature is to be non-existent, like a flower in the sky, there is nothing for a cause to bring about. Both horns treat the effect as having a fixed nature, of being or of not being. But something that brings about nothing is not a cause. Being a cause is not a property a thing has on its own. It is a name given because an effect arises in dependence on it, as chapter one found. Take away the effect and the cause goes with it. The same holds for the gathering: it does not make itself, and depends on its parts and on the effect it is named for. So the chapter ends: there is no effect made by a gathering, and none made without one; and without an effect, there is no gathering of conditions to speak of.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Flour, water, yeast and heat still make a loaf
Leave out the yeast: a flat loaf
What goes: self-standing ingredients handing over
slides.say: None of this stops the bread from being baked. Flour, water, yeast and heat still go into the oven, and a loaf still comes out. A baker who leaves out the yeast still gets a flat loaf. Every craft and science that tracks what follows from what is left exactly as it was. What goes is a picture laid over the baking: a collection of self-standing ingredients that either contains the loaf or hands it something across a gap in time. When cause and effect are taken as designated together, each named in dependence on the other, the puzzles of contact, handover and timing never arise. As Tsongkhapa puts it, what reasoning negates is production established by its own nature, not production as the world speaks of it.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Look for the moment dough becomes bread
Look for the yeast's power passing into the loaf
Yet the bread is there, warm, and it feeds you
slides.say: This can be checked in the kitchen. Look for the moment when the dough becomes bread. Look for the place where the yeast's power passes into the loaf. Every moment is full of change, and at no moment is a finished loaf handed across from one thing to another. Yet the bread is there, warm, and it feeds you.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: the Interlude; Chapters 3 and 4
The Logic of Dependency: the eight extremes
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: the Interlude, on conditions and causes; chapter three, on appearances present without being produced; and chapter four, on the problem of interaction and how things meet, neither one nor two. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, turns over identity and difference: the sprout is not the seed, and yet rice yields rice. Links to all of them are on the chapter page.
